title: Failed Window Seals & Flashing: Slow Water Intrusion | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: Why window seals and flashing fail, how slow leaks hide inside walls, and what the stains, soft drywall, and peeling paint around a window are telling you.
h1: Failed Window Seals & Flashing as a Slow Water Intrusion Path
intro: You have painted that corner below the window twice now. Maybe three times. The paint goes on fine, it looks right for a season, and then the same faint brown line comes back through, a little wider than last time. Nobody in the house has spilled anything there. The roof was looked at. It only seems to show up after a real storm, and by the time you get around to thinking about it, the wall is dry again and it feels silly to call anyone. So it sits. And somewhere underneath the annoyance is a quieter question you have not said out loud, which is: what is actually happening inside that wall, and how long has it been happening?

sections.heading: A window does not keep water out by being sealed shut
sections.body: Most people picture a window as a plug in a hole, held in place by caulk. That is not how a wall assembly is designed to work. A properly installed window sheds water in layers. There is a sill pan or flashing under the window that catches anything getting past the frame and directs it back out. There is flashing tape or metal at the head and jambs, lapped shingle-style so water running down the wall goes over the top of the layer below it, not behind it. There is a weather-resistive barrier behind the siding or stucco. Caulk is the outermost layer and the least important one, a sacrificial bead, not the system. When someone says a window leaked, what usually failed is not the glass. It is the order of those layers, or the fact that the sill was never pan-flashed to begin with, or that a remodel cut into the barrier and taped over it instead of lapping it correctly. Water then follows gravity and capillary action into the framing, and it does not announce itself. It travels down a stud, soaks the bottom plate, and shows up on drywall three feet from where it entered.

sections.heading: Why desert construction hides this longer than you would expect
sections.body: Slow window leaks behave differently here than they do in a wet climate. Sun exposure is the driver. Ultraviolet light and heat cycling break down sealant and the adhesive on flashing tape faster than moisture ever would, so the failure often begins during the dry months when nothing is leaking at all. Frames expand and contract every single day between a hot afternoon and a cool night, which works old caulk loose at the corners. Then monsoon season arrives with wind-driven rain hitting the wall sideways rather than falling straight down, and water gets pushed uphill into gaps that would never leak in a calm rain. Stucco makes it harder to see. Stucco absorbs water and holds it, so a wall can be wet behind the finish while the outside looks dusty and dry an hour later. Between storms, the dry air pulls the surface moisture out and the stain fades, which is exactly why the problem feels intermittent and unserious. What dries out is the paint. What often does not fully dry is the sheathing, the bottom plate, and the insulation sitting in the wall cavity where no air moves.

sections.heading: Signs worth taking seriously, in the order they usually appear
sections.body: Slow intrusion tends to show a sequence, and knowing the sequence tells you roughly how far along you are. Early: caulk at the window perimeter has hairline cracks or has pulled away from the frame on one side, usually the side that gets the most afternoon sun. Paint on the interior sill or the drywall return looks slightly chalky or has small bubbles. Middle: a stain at the bottom corners of the window that reappears after rain, baseboard that has swelled or lifted at the seam, drywall tape starting to lift where the wall meets the window return, a musty smell that is stronger with the blinds closed. Later: drywall that feels soft or gives under thumb pressure, flooring that has cupped or lifted along the wall line, visible dark spotting on the wall or on the underside of the sill, tile or laminate popping loose near the base. A useful test at any stage: press firmly along the drywall directly under the window and then a foot to each side. Firm wall that goes slightly spongy in one spot means the moisture is inside the cavity, not on the surface. Also check the exterior after a storm and look for a rust line, a chalky white mineral streak, or a stucco crack running down from a window corner. Those corners are where stress concentrates, and a crack there is a direct path in.

cards.heading: Stain that keeps returning through paint
cards.body: Repainting seals nothing. If tannins or minerals keep bleeding through the same spot, water is still arriving there and the source is behind the drywall.

cards.heading: Damage below the window, not at it
cards.body: Water enters high and exits low. Swollen baseboard or cupped flooring under a window with a dry-looking sill still points at the window as the entry.

cards.heading: Only after wind-driven rain
cards.body: A leak that appears only in certain storms usually means a directional flashing gap, not a plumbing problem. Note which direction the rain came from.

cards.heading: Smell before sight
cards.body: An earthy or musty odor near a window with no visible stain often means the cavity has been damp for a while and the drywall has simply not saturated through yet.

sections.heading: Why the repair is usually bigger than the caulk gun
sections.body: The hard part of this problem is not fixing it, it is accepting the scope. Re-caulking the outside of a window that is leaking through failed flashing will stop the visible drip for a while and hide the ongoing damage for longer. Worse, sealing the outside can trap water that was previously finding its way back out. Doing it properly generally means opening the wall to find out how far the moisture traveled, drying the framing and sheathing to a stable moisture level rather than a dry-to-the-touch level, removing insulation that has been wet (fiberglass that has been soaked does not recover its performance and holds moisture against the framing), correcting the flashing and the drainage plane at the window itself, and then rebuilding the wall, texture, and paint so the repair does not read as a patch. That last part is where a lot of homeowners get stranded, with a dried-out hole in the wall and a separate search for someone to close it up. faqs.q: Can I just re-caulk the window myself and see if it stops?
faqs.a: You can, and on a window where the only issue is a cracked exterior bead with no interior signs, that may genuinely be enough. Remove the old caulk completely rather than laying new over it, and use a sealant rated for exterior use and sun exposure. But if you already have interior stains, soft drywall, swollen baseboard, or a musty smell, caulk is treating the symptom. Those signs mean water has already gotten past the outer layer and is inside the wall assembly, and sealing the outside can slow its ability to drain back out.

faqs.q: The stain dries up completely between storms. Does that mean the wall is drying out too?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Painted drywall surfaces dry quickly in Arizona's air. The framing, sheathing, and insulation behind it sit in a closed cavity with almost no airflow and hold moisture far longer. It is common for a surface to look and feel dry while the material behind it is still wet. That difference is why the problem feels occasional from the outside while damage accumulates steadily underneath.

faqs.q: How do I tell a window leak from a plumbing leak in the same wall?
faqs.a: Timing is the strongest clue. A leak that only appears or worsens within a day of rain, and especially after wind-driven rain from one particular direction, points to the building envelope. A leak that is steady regardless of weather, or that changes with water use in the house, points to supply or drain plumbing. Bathrooms and kitchens complicate this because both can be true at once. If the wall has a window and a wet wall, both should be checked before anything is closed up.
